youtube.baslik: Switch-On and Mapping: T and C/M Levels | Lesson 242 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
How is a cochlear implant switched on for the first time, and how is a personal map created? In this lesson we cover threshold (T) and comfort (C/M) levels, the electrical dynamic range, the input dynamic range, loudness balancing, pulse width and the compliance limit, the switch-on experience and counseling.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Wolfe, Cochlear Implants: Audiologic Management and Considerations for Implantable Hearing Devices; Wolfe and Schafer, Programming Cochlear Implants; Zeng et al. (2002), Speech dynamic range and its effect on cochlear implant performance, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: T and C/M levels, the map
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how a cochlear implant is switched on for the first time and how a personal map is created.
We will cover threshold and comfort levels, the electrical dynamic range and counseling on the day of switch-on.
The internal unit is placed in surgery, but since the external unit is not yet worn, the person hears nothing through the implant yet.
There is usually a wait of a few weeks for the wound to heal and swelling to settle; this period varies between centers.
Some centers can activate a few days after surgery if the skin allows.
On switch-on day, the audiologist fits the external unit, makes measurements and creates the first map.
People often describe these first sounds as strange, mechanical or like beeps.
Frequent visits follow in the first months, because levels change as the person gets used to electrical stimulation.
Before measurements, the skin where the coil will sit is examined; if the wound has not healed or there is redness, the team is informed.
The strength of the magnet holding the coil is chosen for each person; a magnet that is too strong can cause pressure sores on the skin.
A weak magnet, on the other hand, makes the coil fall off often and interrupts stimulation.
Then impedance is measured again by telemetry, and electrodes with open or short circuits are identified.
The person and family are told in advance what will happen today, how the first sounds may come across, and that this is normal.
This short preparation reduces anxiety and helps the person respond more reliably during measurements.
Programming is based on finding two levels for each electrode; the graph shows how loudness grows as current increases.
The threshold level, or T level, is the lowest current level at which the stimulus is barely detected.
Some centers define the T level as the level detected half the time, others as the level detected every time.
The comfort level, or C level, is the highest level at which sound is loud but still comfortable.

cumleler.yazi: In some systems the upper level is defined as the most comfortable listening level and called the M level; hence the term C/M level.
cumleler.ses: In some systems the upper level is defined as the most comfortable listening level and called the M level; hence the term C or M level.

cumleler.yazi: The range between T and C/M is the electrical dynamic range, and it is often only about 10 to 20 decibels.
cumleler.ses: The range between T and C or M is the electrical dynamic range, and it is often only about 10 to 20 decibels.

cumleler: Compared with the natural ear's range of about 120 decibels, it is clear why the implant has to compress.
To measure the T level, current starts at a low level where the stimulus is not heard and is raised in small steps.
The stimulus is usually given as short trains of beeps; the person signals or presses a button when they hear it.
Adults may also be asked to count how many beeps they heard; this reduces the tendency to guess.
In some systems T levels are not measured one by one; the software sets them as a fraction of the upper level, then fine-tuning follows.
If T levels are set too high, soft ambient sounds and hum are heard constantly and can be annoying.
If they are set too low, soft speech and distant sounds may be missed.
So T levels are confirmed with the aided thresholds we will see below and with the person's daily experience.
To measure the C or M level, the person is shown an illustrated loudness scale ordered from very soft to too loud.
The person is asked to point to where the sound falls on the scale and to report the loud but comfortable point.
Current is raised toward this point in small, careful steps; a sudden loud stimulus can startle the person.
Meanwhile the person's face is watched; blinking or twitching of facial muscles may show that stimulation is spreading to the facial nerve.
A very strong stimulus can also cause discomfort, pain or nonauditory sensations such as dizziness.
On the first day, the person is not used to electrical stimulation, so upper levels are often set cautiously, that is, lower than needed.
As the person adapts, upper levels are raised step by step at later visits.

cumleler.yazi: Together, the T and C/M levels of all electrodes make up the person's map, that is, their program.
cumleler.ses: Together, the T and C or M levels of all electrodes make up the person's map, that is, their program.

cumleler: In this example, the navy line shows the T levels across the electrodes.

cumleler.yazi: The blue line shows the C/M levels; both lines vary a little from electrode to electrode.
cumleler.ses: The blue line shows the C or M levels; both lines vary a little from electrode to electrode.

cumleler: The distance between the two lines is the dynamic range of each electrode.
Levels vary between people and between electrodes; the state of the nerve fibers and the electrode's distance from the modiolus affect this.
The map is saved in the programming software and loaded into the sound processor.
A processor can store more than one map, for example several programs for different environments.

ogeler.metin: Should fall from base to apex

cumleler: After the levels are measured one by one, neighboring electrodes are played in sequence and the person is asked to compare their loudness.
If one is clearly louder or softer than another, its level is corrected; this is called loudness balancing.
In adults the pitch order of electrodes can also be checked; pitch should rise toward the base.
Some electrodes can stimulate the facial nerve and cause eye or facial twitching; these are switched off or their levels limited.
Electrodes that cause pain, dizziness or a nonauditory sensation are handled the same way.
Electrodes with open or short circuits are removed from the map, and the frequency bands are spread over the remaining electrodes.

x.ad: Sound level at the microphone (dB SPL)

cumleler: So how do these levels relate to real sounds?

cumleler.yazi: The processor converts the sound level at the microphone into a current between T and C/M according to this curve.
cumleler.ses: The processor converts the sound level at the microphone into a current between T and C or M according to this curve.

cumleler: The range of sound that is mapped is called the input dynamic range, for example from 25 to 85 decibels.
Soft sounds at the lower end of the range are delivered close to the T level, that is, barely audible.

cumleler.yazi: Loud sounds at the upper end are mapped to the C/M level; louder sounds do not exceed this level, that is, they are clipped.
cumleler.ses: Loud sounds at the upper end are mapped to the C or M level; louder sounds do not exceed this level, that is, they are clipped.

cumleler: Because the curve is logarithmic, a larger share of the electrical range goes to soft and moderate sounds.
The width of the input range and the microphone sensitivity clearly affect how well the person hears soft sounds.
What determines nerve stimulation is the electric charge in the pulse; charge is current multiplied by pulse duration.
So loudness can be increased by raising the current or by making the pulse longer.
On an electrode with high impedance, the voltage needed for the desired current may exceed what the implant can supply.
In that case the software widens the pulse to deliver the same charge with less current, and loudness is maintained.
A wider pulse makes each cycle longer, which can lower the pulse rate per channel.
Programming software usually flags electrodes that are approaching this limit.
When the map is ready, the microphone is turned on and the person begins to hear surrounding sounds, above all speech, through the implant.

cumleler.yazi: If overall loudness is not comfortable in live sound, all C/M levels are lowered or raised a little together.
cumleler.ses: If overall loudness is not comfortable in live sound, all C or M levels are lowered or raised a little together.

cumleler: If soft sounds are not heard at all, the T levels and microphone sensitivity are reviewed.
The audiologist speaks at soft and normal levels and watches the person's reactions and comfort.
The sounds of the Ling six sound test give a quick check of whether speech frequencies are heard.
Finally, one or more programs are loaded into the processor, and the person is shown how to change volume and programs.
The frequency allocation table determines which frequency band goes to which electrode.
This table is usually used in its default form; changes are made carefully, because they change the pitch of sounds.
Microphone sensitivity and directional microphone settings affect how much soft sound and noise from behind is picked up.
Noise reduction and programs that change automatically with the environment are used much as in hearing aids.
In the first weeks, some centers load several maps together with gradually increasing upper levels.
The person moves to the next map every few days, so loudness increases without waiting for the next visit.
The most important message of the first day is that it is expected for sounds to seem strange.
Speech may not be understood at first; the brain adapts to this new code over weeks and months.
This adaptation requires regular use of the processor during all waking hours; data logging shows the hours of use.
The person is taught to change batteries, check the cable and coil, and protect the processor from moisture.
They are told to remove the processor and contact the center if loudness is uncomfortable, or if pain or facial twitching occurs.
At home, talking with family about familiar topics and matching sounds to their sources speeds up adaptation in the first weeks.
This graph shows the typical course of levels in the first year with example values; upper levels rise clearly in the first months.
T levels change less; levels largely stabilize within roughly a few months.
So the first maps are temporary and are updated as the person adapts.
Visits are frequent in the first few months, for example a few weeks apart; then the intervals lengthen to yearly checks.
At each visit impedance is measured, levels are reviewed, and aided thresholds and speech tests are done.
The visit schedule varies with the center and the person's progress; children need more frequent visits.

sahneler.metin: Watch the person's face while raising upper levels. If you see blinking or twitching, stop on that electrode; this can come before any report of loudness.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: when raising upper levels, take your eyes off the screen and look at the person's face.
Blinking or cheek twitching may show facial nerve stimulation, and the person may not always mention it.
If you see this, stop raising the level on that electrode and assess it together with the team.
This may be more common in people with otosclerosis, inner ear malformations or a temporal bone fracture.

maddeler.metin: Levels change in the first months

cumleler: The T level is the lowest level at which electrical stimulation is barely detected.
The C or M level is the upper level, loud but comfortable; the narrow range between them is the electrical dynamic range.
The levels of all electrodes, balancing, the mapping curve and other settings together make up the person's map.
Levels change as the person adapts to electrical stimulation, so frequent programming and counseling are needed in the first months.

sahneler.soru: What does a constant hum in quiet suggest?
sahneler.aciklama: If _T levels_ are high, soft sounds and hum are heard constantly.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: an implant user reports a constant hum in a quiet room; which setting comes to mind first?

cumleler: The correct answer is A: T levels set too high.
When T levels are set high, soft ambient sounds and system noise may be heard constantly, so the levels are reviewed.
In the next lesson we will learn about programming in children, predicting the map from objective measures, and behavioral confirmation.
